items.title: Rufus Reid interviewed by Monk Rowe, Atlanta, GA, January 4, 2013
items.q: we had Benny Golson wrote for the orchestra, and he wrote a concerto for me, and he wrote pieces for himself, and we did a thing at Alice Tully Hall with the William Chamber Orchestra.

ctx.x: Wow. I’ve been lucky to have a couple of those people too, so, I’m glad you got to speak about him.

Yeah. Because we all have to survive. We all have to — but when you can find someone who really — and I never knew what that word meant — someone who champions you. Someone who really champions you. He was the one that actually, because we were the first to get – William Paterson was the first to get the Doris Duke Award. items.title: Benny Golson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Sometimes we used Ray Drummond as a bass player, Rufus Reid as a bass player... We got together again. The front line was the same... But the rhythm section changed then.

ctx.x: We went our separate ways, Art and I and all of us, doing this and doing that. We figured out we’d done what we wanted to do with the Jazztet. It was not earthshaking. It didn’t change the cosmic balance of the universe or anything like that. So we went our separate ways. But years later, we got the taste again. Maybe we can do something a little different this time, and we did. We got together again. The front line was the same: Art Farmer, Curtis Fuller, and me. But the rhythm section changed then. So much time…
